subtopic_detail: Prosthetic valve endocarditis with new regurgitation and pulmonary oedema after antibiotics were started in the community
stem:
You are the medical registrar caring for a 62 year old man on day two of an admission with three weeks of fevers and drenching night sweats. He received a bioprosthetic aortic valve fourteen months ago and his general practitioner prescribed oral amoxicillin four days before admission for presumed sinusitis.

Overnight he has become breathless lying flat and now needs 6 L of oxygen by mask, with bibasal crackles to the mid zones and a new early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge. Three sets of blood cultures taken on admission remain sterile. Transoesophageal echocardiography this morning shows a 12 mm vegetation on the prosthetic aortic valve, severe aortic regurgitation and an echo lucent cavity at the aortic root consistent with an abscess. He has been on empirical vancomycin and gentamicin since admission.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 118 per minute, blood pressure 104/44 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 per minute, SpO2 91 per cent on 6 L per minute by mask, temperature 38.6 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 17.4 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), C reactive protein 186 mg/L (less than 5), creatinine 128 micromol/L (60-110), three sets of blood cultures sterile at 48 hours
data_table.Imaging: Transoesophageal echocardiography shows a 12 mm prosthetic aortic valve vegetation, severe aortic regurgitation and an aortic root abscess cavity

lead_in: What is the most important next step in his management?

options.text: Continue the current antimicrobials and reassess him after completing six weeks of therapy
options.rationale: Antibiotics cannot reverse mechanical valve failure and the abscess will continue to extend into the root while therapy runs. A full medical course alone suits uncomplicated native valve disease with a stable valve and no heart failure (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Cease all antibiotics for 48 hours so that further blood cultures can be taken while he is untreated
options.rationale: Deliberate antibiotic interruption to improve culture yield is only considered in a haemodynamically stable patient with an indolent illness, and here it risks rapid deterioration. Serology and molecular testing on excised tissue answer the culture negative question more safely (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Add high dose rifampicin to the regimen to improve penetration of the prosthetic valve material
options.rationale: Rifampicin is used against staphylococcal prosthetic material infection once bacteraemia has cleared, but adding it does nothing for the acute regurgitation flooding his lungs. Its addition is a decision for after the surgical plan is made and an organism is known (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Refer him immediately for cardiac surgery with a view to valve replacement and root repair
options.rationale: Heart failure from severe valvular regurgitation is the strongest indication for emergency surgery in endocarditis, and perivalvular abscess in a prosthetic valve is an independent indication in its own right. Delaying for a longer antibiotic course in this setting is associated with markedly higher mortality (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).
source_refs: European Society of Cardiology: Guidelines on infective endocarditis

options.text: Start therapeutic anticoagulation with heparin to reduce the risk of systemic embolism from the vegetation
options.rationale: Anticoagulation does not reduce embolic risk from vegetations and increases the chance of haemorrhagic transformation if a septic embolus has already reached the brain. The measure that lowers embolic risk here is removal of the vegetation at operation (Source: European Society of Cardiology: Guidelines on infective endocarditis).
source_refs: European Society of Cardiology: Guidelines on infective endocarditis

explanation.summary: About half of patients with infective endocarditis need surgery, and the three broad indications are heart failure from valve dysfunction, uncontrolled infection such as abscess or persistent bacteraemia, and prevention of embolism from a large mobile vegetation. Heart failure is the most urgent of these and drives operation within hours to days rather than after a completed antibiotic course. Prosthetic valve involvement raises the threshold for cure with antibiotics alone and lowers the threshold for surgery. Culture negative disease is common when antibiotics have been given before sampling and is investigated with serology for Coxiella and Bartonella plus molecular testing of excised valve tissue. Early involvement of an endocarditis team improves outcomes because the decision is rarely a single specialty one.
key_points: Heart failure from acute valvular regurgitation is the leading indication for urgent surgery
Perivalvular abscess signals uncontrolled infection and is a separate surgical indication
Prosthetic valve endocarditis is far less often cured by antibiotics alone
Prior community antibiotics are the commonest reason blood cultures are sterile
Anticoagulation does not prevent embolism from vegetations and adds haemorrhagic risk
explanation.pearls: A new regurgitant murmur with pulmonary oedema in suspected endocarditis mandates a surgical conversation the same day, since operating before multiorgan failure develops is the single largest modifiable determinant of survival.

sources.label: European Society of Cardiology: Guidelines on infective endocarditis

subtopic_detail: Timing of antiretroviral therapy in a newly diagnosed patient being treated for cryptococcal meningitis
stem:
You are the infectious diseases registrar looking after a 38 year old man diagnosed with human immunodeficiency virus infection nine days ago after presenting with headache and confusion. His CD4 count is 28 cells per microlitre and his viral load is 420 000 copies per mL.

Cerebrospinal fluid on admission grew Cryptococcus neoformans with an opening pressure of 34 cmH2O, and he has had daily therapeutic lumbar punctures. He is on day five of liposomal amphotericin B with flucytosine and his headache and conscious state have improved markedly. He has no tuberculosis symptoms, a normal chest radiograph and a negative urinary lipoarabinomannan test. His renal function and potassium are being replaced and remain stable, and he is keen to begin treatment for the virus as soon as possible.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 82 per minute, blood pressure 118/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 37.0 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: CD4 count 28 cells per microlitre, HIV viral load 420 000 copies per mL, cerebrospinal fluid culture positive for Cryptococcus neoformans, opening pressure 34 cmH2O at diagnosis, creatinine 92 micromol/L (60-110), potassium 3.8 mmol/L (3.5-5.2)
data_table.Imaging: Chest radiograph normal, computed tomography of the brain shows no focal lesion or hydrocephalus

lead_in: When should antiretroviral therapy be started?

options.text: Today, because a CD4 count below 50 cells per microlitre makes any delay in treatment unsafe
options.rationale: A very low CD4 count is exactly the situation in which early antiretroviral therapy during cryptococcal meningitis increased mortality in randomised trials, driven by immune reconstitution inflammatory disease in a closed cranial compartment. Same day initiation is the correct instinct for most other new diagnoses (Source: ASHM: Antiretroviral guidelines).

options.text: Once the induction antifungal course finishes at two weeks, provided the repeat culture is sterile
options.rationale: Two weeks still falls inside the window where excess deaths were observed, and cerebrospinal fluid sterility at the end of induction does not remove that risk. Culture conversion guides antifungal stepdown rather than the timing of antiretroviral therapy (Source: ASHM: Antiretroviral guidelines).

options.text: Only after the full twelve month course of maintenance fluconazole has been successfully completed
options.rationale: Withholding therapy for a year leaves him profoundly immunosuppressed and exposed to further opportunistic disease, which is a far greater hazard than the reconstitution syndrome. Maintenance antifungal treatment runs concurrently with antiretroviral therapy rather than before it (Source: ASHM: Antiretroviral guidelines).

options.text: Immediately, but with a corticosteroid started alongside it to prevent an inflammatory reaction
options.rationale: Adjunctive corticosteroids in cryptococcal meningitis worsened outcomes and increased adverse events in a randomised trial, so they do not license early initiation. Steroids are reserved for established severe reconstitution disease with mass effect (Source: ASHM: Antiretroviral guidelines).

options.text: After four to six weeks of antifungal therapy, once his intracranial pressure has been controlled
options.rationale: Deferring antiretroviral therapy for four to six weeks after starting antifungal treatment reduced mortality compared with early initiation in cryptococcal meningitis, because reconstituted inflammation inside the skull raises pressure catastrophically. This is a deliberate exception to the same day start recommended for almost every other new diagnosis (Source: ASHM: Antiretroviral guidelines).
source_refs: New England Journal of Medicine: COAT trial of antiretroviral timing in cryptococcal meningitis

explanation.summary: Rapid or same day antiretroviral initiation is now standard for new human immunodeficiency virus diagnoses because it improves retention in care and reduces transmission, but two central nervous system infections are recognised exceptions. In cryptococcal meningitis, starting within the first fortnight increased mortality in a randomised trial through immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome in a space that cannot expand. Tuberculous meningitis carries a similar concern and is usually managed with a delay of several weeks. Control of raised intracranial pressure with repeated therapeutic lumbar puncture is the intervention with the largest short term survival benefit in cryptococcal disease, ahead of the choice of antifungal. Once therapy does begin, maintenance fluconazole continues until the CD4 count has recovered above 100 cells per microlitre with viral suppression for at least three months.
key_points: Defer antiretroviral therapy four to six weeks in cryptococcal meningitis despite a very low CD4 count
The mechanism is immune reconstitution inflammation within a non expandable cranial compartment
Therapeutic lumbar puncture for raised opening pressure is the highest yield acute intervention
Adjunctive corticosteroids worsen outcomes in cryptococcal meningitis
Same day initiation remains the default for new diagnoses without a central nervous system opportunistic infection
explanation.pearls: Repeat therapeutic lumbar puncture whenever the opening pressure exceeds 25 cmH2O, draining to about half the opening value or until the pressure is below 20 cmH2O, because pressure control saves more lives early than any change of antifungal.

sources.label: New England Journal of Medicine: COAT trial of antiretroviral timing in cryptococcal meningitis

subtopic_detail: Painful desquamating rash with mucosal ulceration three weeks after an anticonvulsant was introduced
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar seeing a 34 year old woman brought in by her partner with two days of fever and a spreading rash that she describes as feeling like scalding. She started lamotrigine three weeks ago for bipolar disorder and the dose was increased last week.

Her lips are crusted and bleeding, her conjunctivae are injected with adhesions forming at the lid margin, and there are erosions on the buccal mucosa that stop her drinking. Dusky macules with central blistering cover her trunk and proximal arms, and gentle lateral pressure on apparently normal skin at the shoulder shears the epidermis away. You estimate detached and detachable skin at about 12 per cent of body surface area. She has no facial oedema, no lymphadenopathy and no eosinophilia, and her liver enzymes are normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 122 per minute, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 per minute, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 38.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Dusky targetoid macules with blistering over 12 per cent body surface area, positive skin shear sign, haemorrhagic crusting of the lips, ocular and buccal erosions, no facial oedema or lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Eosinophils 0.1 x10^9/L (0.0-0.5), alanine aminotransferase 22 U/L (less than 40), creatinine 104 micromol/L (45-90), bicarbonate 19 mmol/L (22-32)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Cease the lamotrigine and arrange urgent transfer to a burns unit with ophthalmology review
options.rationale: Immediate withdrawal of the causative drug and transfer to a unit experienced in large area skin loss are the two interventions with the clearest survival benefit, and early ocular assessment prevents the adhesions that cause lifelong visual loss. Fluid, temperature and analgesia needs approach those of a thermal burn (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology).
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Burn Association: Guidelines for severe cutaneous adverse reactions

options.text: Reduce the lamotrigine to the previous lower dose and observe her on the medical ward overnight
options.rationale: Dose reduction maintains exposure to the drug driving keratinocyte apoptosis and detachment progresses over the following days regardless of dose. Slower titration prevents this reaction at the point of initiation but has no role once it has begun (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Commence intravenous aciclovir and swab the mucosal lesions for herpes simplex virus testing
options.rationale: Herpes associated erythema multiforme produces true target lesions on the extremities without widespread epidermal detachment, and the shear sign is absent. Antiviral therapy would be appropriate for recurrent herpes triggered disease, not for this drug reaction (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology).

options.text: Start intravenous flucloxacillin for presumed staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome and admit her
options.rationale: The staphylococcal toxin mediated syndrome spares the mucous membranes and occurs almost entirely in young children, whereas mucosal involvement at three sites is the hallmark of this drug reaction. Prophylactic antibiotics are also avoided because they select resistant organisms in denuded skin (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Give a three day course of pulsed intravenous methylprednisolone before any change to her medication
options.rationale: Immunomodulatory therapy remains contested and none of it substitutes for stopping the drug, which must happen first and immediately. Any decision about corticosteroids, ciclosporin or immunoglobulin belongs to the receiving specialist unit (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology).

explanation.summary: Stevens Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis are a single disease separated by the proportion of body surface with epidermal detachment, under 10 per cent, 10 to 30 per cent and over 30 per cent respectively. Anticonvulsants, allopurinol, sulfonamides and nevirapine account for a large share of cases, and lamotrigine risk is strongly related to the speed of dose escalation, particularly alongside valproate. Mortality is predicted by the SCORTEN score using age, malignancy, heart rate, surface area, urea, glucose and bicarbonate measured in the first 24 hours. Care is largely supportive and mirrors burns management, with meticulous fluid balance, warming, analgesia, wound care and daily ophthalmic review. Immunomodulatory options are debated and are decided in specialist units rather than in the emergency department.
key_points: Detachment of 10 to 30 per cent of body surface defines the overlap band between the two named syndromes
Ceasing the causative drug immediately is the intervention most clearly linked to survival
Mucosal involvement at multiple sites distinguishes this from staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome
Daily ophthalmology review prevents symblepharon and long term visual loss
The absence of facial oedema, eosinophilia and hepatitis argues against a drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms
explanation.pearls: Lamotrigine must be titrated over at least six weeks, and the starting dose is halved again when valproate is co prescribed, because valproate roughly doubles lamotrigine concentrations and rapid escalation is the dominant risk factor for this reaction.

sources.label: Australian and New Zealand Burn Association: Guidelines for severe cutaneous adverse reactions

subtopic_detail: Symmetrical parkinsonism with early falls and syncope that responds poorly to a full levodopa trial
stem:
You are the general physician reviewing a 66 year old man diagnosed with Parkinson disease eighteen months ago by his general practitioner. He now takes levodopa with carbidopa four times daily at a total daily levodopa dose of 1000 mg, taken reliably.

His wife reports he has fallen backwards eleven times in the past six months and has blacked out three times while standing at the kitchen bench. He has needed a urinary catheter twice for retention and wakes at night with loud snoring and shouting. His movements are stiff and slow on both sides to an equal degree, and there is no tremor at rest. Standing blood pressure falls from 138/82 to 92/58 mmHg after three minutes with no rise in pulse rate. His wife says the medication made no appreciable difference at any dose.

data_table.Vital signs: Supine pulse rate 76 per minute, supine blood pressure 138/82 mmHg, standing blood pressure 92/58 mmHg at 3 minutes with pulse rate 78 per minute, respiratory rate 14 per minute, SpO2 97 per cent on room air
data_table.Examination: Symmetrical rigidity and bradykinesia, no rest tremor, retropulsion on pull testing, normal eye movements in the vertical plane
data_table.Investigations: Full blood examination, electrolytes, thyroid function and vitamin B12 within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Increase the total daily levodopa dose further and review his response again in eight weeks
options.rationale: He has already had an adequate trial at a dose where idiopathic disease reliably responds, so escalation adds orthostatic hypotension without benefit. Dose escalation is the right move when there has been partial benefit and wearing off between doses (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

options.text: Refer for neurology assessment with magnetic resonance imaging as the pattern suggests atypical disease
options.rationale: Symmetrical disease without rest tremor, falls within the first year, early autonomic failure and a poor response to an adequate levodopa trial are red flags against idiopathic Parkinson disease and point to a degenerative parkinsonism with autonomic involvement. Specialist confirmation changes prognosis, driving advice and the way autonomic symptoms are managed (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).
source_refs: Movement Disorder Society: Diagnostic criteria for parkinsonian disorders

options.text: Add a dopamine agonist to his regimen and titrate it upwards over the following several weeks
options.rationale: Dopamine agonists worsen orthostatic hypotension and carry impulse control and hallucination risk in this age group, and they will not rescue a syndrome that has not responded to levodopa. They are an option in younger patients with confirmed idiopathic disease (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Commence an anticholinergic agent to target his rigidity and reduce the frequency of his falls
options.rationale: Anticholinergics mainly help tremor, which he does not have, and they precipitate urinary retention and cognitive impairment in older patients. His two episodes of retention make this class particularly hazardous (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Start a cholinesterase inhibitor on the basis that his falls and night time behaviour indicate dementia
options.rationale: Cholinesterase inhibitors are used for established dementia in parkinsonian syndromes, and no cognitive impairment has been documented here. The night time shouting more likely reflects rapid eye movement sleep behaviour disorder, which is a supportive feature rather than an indication for this drug (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

explanation.summary: Idiopathic Parkinson disease is asymmetrical at onset, usually features a rest tremor, and responds convincingly to levodopa, so a patient who fails all three of these expectations deserves diagnostic review rather than more medication. Early postural instability with falls in the first year, prominent autonomic failure with orthostatic hypotension and urinary dysfunction, and rapid progression are the classic red flags for multiple system atrophy and progressive supranuclear palsy. Vertical gaze restriction points to the latter, while marked autonomic involvement and cerebellar signs point to the former. Magnetic resonance imaging supports the distinction and excludes vascular and structural mimics. The practical consequences are substantial, since prognosis, driving capacity and the management of blood pressure and bladder all differ from idiopathic disease.
key_points: Symmetry, absent rest tremor and poor levodopa response are red flags against idiopathic disease
Falls within the first year and early autonomic failure suggest an atypical parkinsonian syndrome
An adequate levodopa trial means a sufficient dose taken reliably before declaring non response
Dopamine agonists and anticholinergics both worsen the autonomic burden in these patients
Rapid eye movement sleep behaviour disorder supports a synucleinopathy but does not identify which one
explanation.pearls: A sustained fall of 20 mmHg systolic or 10 mmHg diastolic within three minutes of standing, without a compensatory rise in heart rate, indicates neurogenic orthostatic hypotension and is one of the strongest bedside pointers away from idiopathic Parkinson disease.

sources.label: Movement Disorder Society: Diagnostic criteria for parkinsonian disorders

subtopic_detail: Heavy bleeding on day twelve after a normal vaginal birth with an open cervical os and a tender uterus
stem:
You are the obstetrics and gynaecology registrar in the emergency department seeing a woman who gave birth vaginally twelve days ago at term. Her lochia had almost stopped but this morning she soaked four maternity pads in two hours and passed two clots the size of a golf ball.

Her labour was spontaneous and the placenta was described at the time as appearing complete. She is breastfeeding, has a temperature of 38.2 degrees C and says her lower abdomen aches constantly and her discharge has an offensive smell. The uterus is palpable midway to the umbilicus and is tender, and the cervical os admits a fingertip. She is not dizzy at present and the bleeding has slowed to moderate. Her haemoglobin is 96 g/L and her white cell count is 16.8 x10^9/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 104 per minute, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 38.2 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Uterus palpable midway between symphysis and umbilicus and tender, offensive lochia, cervical os admits a fingertip, no vulval haematoma
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 96 g/L (115-155), white cell count 16.8 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), C reactive protein 88 mg/L (less than 5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Give a single dose of intramuscular ergometrine and discharge her with advice to return if bleeding recurs
options.rationale: A uterotonic may slow the bleeding briefly but leaves the infection and any retained tissue untreated, and discharge before source control risks a return with sepsis. Ergometrine is also avoided where blood pressure is raised (Source: RANZCOG: Management of postpartum haemorrhage).

options.text: Take genital tract and blood cultures, start broad spectrum intravenous antibiotics and arrange pelvic ultrasound
options.rationale: Secondary postpartum haemorrhage with fever, uterine tenderness and offensive lochia is treated as endometritis, which frequently coexists with retained products, so antimicrobial therapy and imaging proceed together after cultures. Surgical evacuation is then decided on the ultrasound findings and the response to treatment (Source: RANZCOG: Management of postpartum haemorrhage).

options.text: Take her directly to theatre for immediate suction curettage of the uterine cavity without imaging
options.rationale: Curetting an infected soft postpartum uterus before antibiotics carries a substantial perforation and Asherman risk, and her bleeding is not torrential enough to demand immediate theatre. Emergency evacuation without imaging is reserved for haemodynamic instability (Source: RANZCOG: Management of postpartum haemorrhage).

options.text: Prescribe oral amoxicillin alone and review her again in general practice within the next two days
options.rationale: Narrow oral therapy does not cover the anaerobes and Gram negative organisms typical of postpartum endometritis, and her tachycardia with a raised inflammatory response warrants parenteral treatment. Oral therapy suits mild afebrile endometritis diagnosed early (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Arrange transfusion of two units of packed red cells and repeat her full blood count in the morning
options.rationale: Transfusion treats a number rather than the cause and is not indicated at this haemoglobin in a woman who is not compromised, with oral or intravenous iron the appropriate replacement. It would be considered if bleeding continued with haemodynamic compromise (Source: National Blood Authority: Patient blood management guidelines).
source_refs: National Blood Authority: Patient blood management guidelines

explanation.summary: Secondary postpartum haemorrhage is bleeding between 24 hours and twelve weeks after birth and is most often caused by endometritis, retained products of conception, or both together, with rarer causes including a uterine arteriovenous malformation and gestational trophoblastic disease. Fever, uterine tenderness and offensive lochia point to infection, while an open cervical os and clot passage raise the probability of retained tissue. Ultrasound cannot reliably separate retained products from clot in the early puerperium, so findings are interpreted alongside the clinical picture rather than as a definitive test. Antibiotic therapy is started before any surgical evacuation because operating on an infected uterus increases perforation and adhesion risk. Persistent or heavy bleeding despite therapy is the trigger for evacuation, usually under ultrasound guidance.
key_points: Bleeding from 24 hours to twelve weeks postpartum is secondary postpartum haemorrhage
Endometritis and retained products commonly coexist and are treated together
Cultures precede antibiotics, and parenteral therapy is used when systemically unwell
Ultrasound findings in the puerperium are interpreted with caution because clot mimics retained tissue
Evacuation follows antibiotic cover unless bleeding is torrential
explanation.pearls: Send a high vaginal swab and blood cultures before the first antibiotic dose, and cover anaerobes explicitly, because Bacteroides and other anaerobic organisms are recovered in a large share of postpartum endometritis and are missed by amoxicillin alone.

sources.label: National Blood Authority: Patient blood management guidelines
